title: Scalar Product of Vectors
short_intro: The scalar product, or dot product, of two vectors is defined as the product of their magnitudes multiplied by the cosine of the angle between them, resulting in a scalar quantity. It serves as a fundamental mathematical operation in mechanics for determining work, potential energy, and projections.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Geometric interpretation, orthogonal conditions, calculation of work done by constant forces, and projection of one vector onto another.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Application to central forces, work-energy theorem derivation, differentiation of scalar products with respect to time, and utilization in conservative force fields.

prerequisites: Definition of vector and scalar quantities
Vector addition and resolution into Cartesian components

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Algebraic Representation
bullets: The scalar product of two vectors A and B is written as A · B = AB cos θ.
In Cartesian coordinate systems, A · B = AxBx + AyBy + AzBz.

concept_notes.heading: Orthogonality and Parallelism
bullets: For orthogonal vectors (θ = 90°), the scalar product is zero: î · ĵ = ĵ · k̂ = k̂ · î = 0.
For parallel vectors (θ = 0°), the scalar product equals the product of their magnitudes: î · î = ĵ · ĵ = k̂ · k̂ = 1.
If A · B = 0 for non-zero vectors, the vectors are strictly perpendicular.

concept_notes.heading: Geometric Interpretation and Projection
bullets: Geometrically, A · B represents the product of the magnitude of A and the scalar component of B along A (B cos θ).
The scalar projection of vector B onto vector A is given by (B · A) / A.
It determines whether the angle between two vectors is acute (θ < 90°, dot product > 0), obtuse (θ > 90°, dot product < 0), or right angle (θ = 90°, dot product = 0).

concept_notes.heading: Distributive Law over Vector Addition
bullets: The scalar product obeys the distributive law: A · (B + C) = (A · B) + (A · C).
This property allows the expansion of dot products using Cartesian unit vector components.
It is essential in computing work done when forces are expressed as sums of orthogonal components.

derivations.title: Cartesian Expansion of Scalar Product
derivations.conditions: Vectors given in terms of orthogonal unit vectors î, ĵ, k̂
steps: Write vectors in component form: A = Axî + Ayĵ + Azk̂ and B = Bxî + Byĵ + Bzk̂.
Apply the distributive law: A · B = (Axî + Ayĵ + Azk̂) · (Bxî + Byĵ + Bzk̂).
Expand the cross terms and apply orthonormal conditions: î · î = 1, î · ĵ = 0, etc.

derivations.title: Work Done by a Constant Force using Scalar Product
derivations.conditions: Particle displaced by displacement vector s under a constant force F
steps: Express work W as the product of the component of force along the displacement and the magnitude of displacement.
Let θ be the angle between force vector F and displacement vector s.
Write the definition of scalar product: W = (F cos θ)s.

formula_sheet.name: Definition of Scalar Product
formula_sheet.variables: A, B = magnitudes of vectors; \theta = angle between them

formula_sheet.name: Cartesian Component Form
formula_sheet.equation_html: A \cdot B = A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z
formula_sheet.variables: A_x, A_y, A_z and B_x, B_y, B_z = rectangular components

formula_sheet.name: Angle Between Two Vectors
formula_sheet.equation_html: \cos \theta = \frac{A \cdot B}{AB} = \frac{A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z}{\sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2} \sqrt{B_x^2 + B_y^2 + B_z^2}}

graphs_and_experiments.title: Geometric Projection Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Vector A along the x-axis and vector B making an angle θ with A, showing the drop-down perpendicular for B cos θ.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how the scalar product multiplies the magnitude of A by the scalar projection of B onto A.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in identifying components of vectors along specific axes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Work vs Displacement Angle Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A cosine curve plotting Work W = Fs cos θ on the y-axis against angle θ (from 0 to 180°) on the x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows positive work for 0° < θ < 90°, zero work at θ = 90°, and negative work for 90° < θ < 180°.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly applied in mechanics problems involving variable force orientation.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Power in Central Force Fields
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Force vector F directed towards a center and velocity vector v tangent to the orbit, with angle θ between them.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: When motion is purely circular under a central force, θ = 90°, making F · v = 0 (zero instantaneous power).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Important for analyzing central force motion and orbital mechanics in PGT exams.

solved_numericals.question: Find the angle between the two vectors A = 3î + 4ĵ + 5k̂ and B = 3î + 4ĵ - 5k̂.
Determine the work done by a force F = 2î - 3ĵ + k̂ N in displacing a particle from position r1 = î + 2ĵ - k̂ m to r2 = 3î + ĵ + 2k̂ m.
solution_steps: Find the displacement vector s = r2 - r1 = (3-1)î + (1-2)ĵ + (2-(-1))k̂ = 2î - ĵ + 3k̂ m.

solved_numericals.question: Find the value of constant 'c' such that the vectors A = 2î - cĵ + k̂ and B = î + 2ĵ - 3k̂ are mutually perpendicular.
solution_steps: For mutually perpendicular vectors, the scalar product must be zero: A · B = 0.
Compute the dot product in component form: (2)(1) + (-c)(2) + (1)(-3) = 0.

assumptions_and_limitations: The scalar product is defined strictly for vectors operating in Euclidean spaces of dimension 3 (or n-dimensional vector spaces with a positive-definite metric).

common_misconceptions.wrong: The scalar product of two vectors can result in a vector pointing along a new direction.
common_misconceptions.correct: The scalar product always yields a scalar real number, never a vector.
common_misconceptions.why: By definition, multiplying magnitudes and the cosine of the angle collapses directional vectors into a single scalar magnitude.

common_misconceptions.wrong: If A · B = A · C, then vector B must equal vector C.
common_misconceptions.correct: Vector B does not necessarily equal vector C.
common_misconceptions.why: The dot product only equates the components along vector A; components perpendicular to A can differ arbitrarily.

quick_revision: The scalar product A · B = AB cos θ is commutative, distributive, and yields zero for orthogonal vectors.
Definition of Scalar Product: A \cdot B = AB \cos \theta
Cartesian Component Form: A \cdot B = A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z
